source.title: Safety Cost of Steering Vectors Is Separable and Reducible

page_placements.theme: Steering for unrelated purposes and generic activation perturbations erode refusal

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates ablation of a known refusal direction by removing it from steering vectors and measuring harmful-request ASR. This is a conceptual test of the direction’s role in safety, but it is not the original intervention of ablating the difference-in-means direction from the residual stream at every layer and position.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own results for refusal-direction ablation in Table 1; those are recorded for V1. Table 4's rank comparison uses CAST-learned safety-degrading directions rather than the known refusal direction, so its findings are recorded under fits_no_version. CAST results, cited findings from other work, and values used only for layer selection are not rows for the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. It never ablates the difference-in-means direction from the model's residual stream, never adds it to induce refusal, and never checks other abilities under that intervention. The 'refusal direction ablation' it runs projects a known refusal direction out of a behavioural steering vector (CAA, one layer). It is a comparator baseline taken from Li et al. (2026) for the paper's own method, CAST. The rows measure how much steering-induced ASR increase is removed by that projection. That is a related but different construct: how far a steering vector's safety cost runs through its overlap with the known direction. It does not show whether the direction mediates refusal in the model. The rank comparison (Table 4, Table 16) varies the rank of learned corrections to a steering vector, not the geometry of the model's refusal representation, so it is not a V4 test either. Findings go to fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that steering-induced safety degradation comes from a separable, mostly rank-1 component of the steering vector, found by constrained primal–dual optimization. Removing it restores safety, including against unseen attacks (GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR), with little loss of steering effect, false refusal or general capability. Projecting out the known refusal direction gives only weak, inconsistent improvement. They add that the learned directions are partly shared across behaviours, and that higher-rank corrections do not improve the trade-off.
record.recipe_differences: The study constructs contrastive steering vectors but learns a safety-degrading direction through constrained optimization, then removes it from the steering vector. It does not test the original difference-in-means refusal direction ablated from model activations at all layers and positions.
record.method_sensitivity: The known-direction ablation results differ by model and by mean versus worst-case ASR: Llama worst-case ASR is largely unchanged, while Qwen-14B worst-case ASR improves more substantially but remains above baseline.

fits_no_version.finding: Projecting the known refusal direction out of benign CAA steering vectors (alpha=1) removes little of the steering-induced ASR increase. Mean ASR: Qwen-7B 35.0→33.6 (baseline 24.5), Qwen-14B 26.8→18.8 (9.0), Llama-8B 12.5→10.8 (1.5). Worst-case ASR barely changes for Qwen-7B and Llama-8B but falls 59.5→35.9 for Qwen-14B. A learned rank-1 direction (CAST) restores ASR to near or below baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The known refusal direction captures only a small part of how benign steering vectors degrade safety; a different learned rank-1 direction captures most of it.

fits_no_version.finding: Rank of the learned removal subspace, Qwen-7B Power-Seeking, alpha=1, change in ASR vs baseline: original +8.9, 1D −6.8, 2D −8.7, 4D −6.8, 8D −6.0. 2D loses effect (+0.49 vs +1.11) and raises FRR (+1.0). For the conciseness vector (Table 16), 1D gives the largest reduction (−12.3); higher ranks give no gain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For correcting steering vectors, a rank-1 learned safety component gives the best safety–utility trade-off; higher ranks add little.

fits_no_version.finding: Learned safety-degrading directions for different behaviours are partly shared: pairwise cosine 0.24–0.84 across models. Their mean, ablated from a held-out sycophancy vector, lowers the ASR increase from +10.6 to +4.7.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-degrading components of different steering vectors occupy a common but not identical subspace.

record.problems: The known-direction ablation results are aggregated across behaviors and attack scenarios, and the paper does not report uncertainty for the ASR values in Table 1. The separate capability evaluation concerns CAST-optimized vectors, not the known-direction ablation.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed CAST ASR results across individual attacks and multipliers (Table 2 and Appendix B.5–B.6) are outcomes of the paper's new learned correction, not the known-direction ablation. General capability results (Appendix B.4) likewise evaluate original steering versus CAST, not the claim's intervention. Table 4's rank comparison is recorded under fits_no_version because it varies the rank of learned safety-degrading components rather than testing refusal-direction geometry.

untested.parts: Not tested: ablating the diff-in-means direction from activations at all layers and positions, adding it to induce refusal, and capability retention under either intervention. The paper also never describes how or at which layer the known refusal direction was computed.
Jailbreaks are evaluation conditions only; no test of whether attacks suppress the direction and no training against its ablation.
Rank comparison concerns learned steering-vector corrections, not the model's refusal geometry. Multi-direction statements are cited from Wollschläger et al. and Pan et al.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'challenges V1' label is withdrawn. The intervention is a projection on a steering vector added at one layer, not directional ablation in the model, so it cannot show whether the direction mediates refusal. The fits_no_version entry cites r7–r11, but those rows are absent from the record's rows list. The refusal direction's derivation (layer, data) is not given in this paper. The direction presumably follows Li et al. (2026).

versions.untested_parts: It does not ablate the difference-in-means direction from every model layer and position or test adding that direction to induce refusal on harmless requests. General capability is not measured for the known-direction ablation.
No conversion of the ablation into a weight edit or evaluation of released abliteration models.
The attacks are evaluation conditions, not tests of whether they suppress the refusal direction; the study does not train against that ablation.
The rank comparison concerns learned safety-degrading components of steering vectors, not whether the model's refusal representation is affine, conic, or a dominant direction plus others.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
No transfer test across languages, base and instruct variants, or other model variants beyond the tested instruct models.
No comparison of safety-training methods or stages for whether a single removable refusal direction exists.

relation.reason: The study cites Arditi et al. for refusal being mediated by a single direction and uses that direction as a comparator tool. Nothing it measures tests the direction's causal role, its multiplicity or its transfer.

tranche.reason: The study uses a known refusal direction only as a baseline mitigation, projected out of CAA steering vectors. It reports ASR for that baseline and for its own learned direction (CAST). It never ablates or adds the direction in model activations, so it gives no result on whether that direction mediates refusal.

source_check.notes: The text never says how the 'refusal direction' baseline was built (prompt sets, layer, difference-in-means). It appears to follow Li et al. 2026. The learned CAST direction is never compared to the known refusal direction by cosine, so the study says nothing about whether they coincide.

statements.correction: Qwen-7B mean 35.0->33.6 (baseline 24.5), about 13% of the rise removed. Llama-8B mean 12.5->10.8 (baseline 1.5), about 15% removed. Qwen-14B mean 26.8->18.8 (baseline 9.0), about 45% removed; Qwen-14B worst case 59.5->35.9 (baseline 20.6). Authors: 'recovering at most 8% on mean ASR'. Steering vectors are CAA vectors for corrigibility, power-seeking and self-awareness. The text does not say how the refusal direction was computed.
statements.problem: All six mean-ASR numbers are correct (Table 1, alpha=1, mean over 3 behaviors x 7 attacks). But 'removes little of the ASR increase' does not fit Qwen-14B. There the projection removes 8.0 of the 17.8-point rise, about 45%, and worst case falls 59.5 to 35.9. The authors call the improvement 'modest' and say worst-case ASR stays largely unchanged on two of the three models.
